# What to do next: make the next experiment auditable

**Research Loop · Piece 03 · As of 2026-10-14 (UTC)**

Google Vids script draft. Approximately 590 spoken words; planned runtime 4:40. Only **Narration** is spoken and used for subtitles. Scene timings are proposed edit timings; **source timestamps** identify the supplied recordings. Use simple diagrams, excerpt cards and text labels; no avatar. This deliverable does not indicate video production or publication.

### Scene 1 · 0:00–0:45 · Choose one bottleneck

<!-- claim_id: 03-c1 -->

**Narration**

Before you delegate a research workflow, choose one narrow, measurable bottleneck. That is our editorial recommendation from the evidence reviewed here, as of October fourteenth, twenty twenty-six.

Periodic Labs’ founders describe full autonomy as a non-goal: automation serves their goals for data. A coding tutorial offers a smaller example, restricting optimization to one instruction file. It changes instructions, not model weights.

The physical-lab advice remains founder testimony. No independent validation of Periodic’s lab performance is supplied. The tutorial illustrates a protocol, but the supplied evidence contains no execution logs.

**Visual**

Title and as-of date, followed by a workflow diagram with one editable box highlighted: `Instruction file → Coding trial → Evaluation`. Label the recommendation **Editorial interpretation** and the interview **Founder testimony**.

Excerpt card: “full autonomy is a non-goal.”

**Sources:** [Periodic interview](https://www.latent.space/p/periodic), source timestamp **50:46–51:39**, `s00230`; [coding tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I), **08:23.00–08:28.16**, `s00108`, and **00:51.34–01:05.64**, `s00010–s00012`.

### Scene 2 · 0:45–1:20 · Keep evaluation separate

<!-- claim_id: 03-c2 -->

**Narration**

Keep final evaluation data and grading authority outside the producing agent’s control. The oversight study supports this separation, and the tutorial makes evaluator checks concrete.

Before launching a search, submit a known broken implementation, a reviewed correct patch, and a forbidden change. Confirm that the evaluator rejects the broken and forbidden cases and accepts the correct one.

These are practical safeguards. They do not guarantee scientific validity. Testing the measuring tool is different from demonstrating that a candidate improved.

**Visual**

Draw two boxes separated by a boundary: `Agent: produces candidate` and `Evaluator: protected data + grading rules`. Animate three labeled test cards: broken → reject; correct → pass; forbidden → reject.

Excerpt: “Protected test data and evaluation criteria should remain outside the producing agent’s control.” Label **Study recommendation**.

**Sources:** [Oversight study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28614), §8, paragraph beginning “These findings support separating research execution”; [tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I), source timestamp **05:27.94–05:43.54**, `s00069–s00071`, with qualification at **05:48.66–05:57.26**, `s00073–s00074`.

### Scene 3 · 1:20–1:55 · Budget the whole comparison

<!-- claim_id: 03-c3 -->

**Narration**

Set a budget for the whole comparison: the baseline, rejected candidates, final checks, and optimizer overhead.

The tutorial’s proposed workload contains thirty-six development trials and twelve final comparison trials. That is forty-eight coding trials before optimizer work, setup, or rehearsals.

The segmentation study caps each campaign at twenty-four logged experiments, including the baseline. Its one-hour training limit applies to an individual trial. Twenty-four experiments must not be presented as a single one-hour search. A candidate’s training budget is only part of the campaign’s cost.

**Visual**

Show `36 development + 12 final = 48 coding trials`, followed by `+ optimizer + setup + rehearsals`. Label **Proposed workload—not an observed execution total**.

Beside it, show twenty-four small trial boxes under a campaign bracket. Excerpt: “Each campaign is capped at 24 logged experiments, including the baseline.”

**Sources:** [Tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I), source timestamp **12:26.58–12:42.38**, `s00162–s00164`; [segmentation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10491), §2, keep/revert rule and campaign cap.

### Scene 4 · 1:55–2:35 · Fix repeat counts in advance

<!-- claim_id: 03-c4 -->

**Narration**

Decide repeat counts before seeing results, and require gains to survive variation before adopting a candidate.

NanoProteinLM’s authors report training every candidate with two seeds, keeping it only when its mean gain exceeds the seed-to-seed spread. The segmentation study does not estimate single-run variation.

The tutorial also contains a contradiction. Its instruction to keep rerunning until lucky conflicts with the adjacent fixed-attempt rule. Do not follow the lucky-rerun instruction.

Our recommendation is to predeclare repetitions. Repeating trials still cannot repair an objective that measures the wrong thing.

**Visual**

Use two seed cards feeding into `Mean gain compared with spread`; label **Author-reported acceptance rule**. Do not invent measured values.

Show adjacent transcript excerpts with a prominent **Contradiction—not recommended practice** label:

- “keep that count unchanged for every candidate.”
- “Keep rerunning one version until it gets lucky.”

**Sources:** [NanoProteinLM author report](https://jojoml.github.io/blog/2026/nanoproteinlm-agenticls/), “What survived the human gate,” first bullet; [segmentation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10491), §3.1, final paragraph; [tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I), source timestamps **08:04.18–08:09.30**, `s00104`, and **08:09.30–08:13.54**, `s00105`. Objective limitation: reviewed brief, “limitations,” and NanoProteinLM, “Failure mode: Perfect on reward, failure on science.”

### Scene 5 · 2:35–3:20 · Preserve executable evidence

<!-- claim_id: 03-c5 -->

**Narration**

Save failed attempts with their exact conditions. For verification, identify the artifact, reproduction configuration, evaluator, and reproduced value.

Agora shows why these details matter. Its account explicitly reports missing evaluator logs and several missing version pins. Its authors did not rerun the winning method.

Our interpretation is to watch for releases that outside researchers can reproduce. A detailed archive does not replace independent replication.

Periodic’s founders also explain why failed synthesis attempts need context. A failure under particular conditions should remain a conditional result, not proof that success is impossible.

**Visual**

Draw a record card: `Artifact hash | Configuration | Evaluator | Reproduced value`. Connect both successful and failed trials to the archive.

Agora excerpt: “We did not rerun the winning method”. Label **Authors’ stated limitation**. A separate card reads **Failed under these conditions**, with the Periodic source timestamp beneath it.

**Sources:** [Agora](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094), Appendix A, verification-record requirements, and §4.8, missing records and no author rerun; [Periodic interview](https://www.latent.space/p/periodic), source timestamps **56:13–56:30**, `s00252`, and **56:33–56:46**, `s00256`.

### Scene 6 · 3:20–4:05 · Test transfer and isolate causes

<!-- claim_id: 03-c6 -->

**Narration**

Look for gains that transfer to protected fresh tasks, and comparisons that isolate the proposed explanation.

In segmentation, coding model and GPU class change together. That prevents attributing the differing outcomes to hardware alone.

In the oversight study, detailed feedback bundles the review decision, reasons, and retained history. Its comparison cannot establish an explanation-specific effect.

The tutorial adds a practical boundary: once final-test feedback guides another revision, those tasks become development data. Reserve new evaluation data. Even then, a small held-out set can leave the result inconclusive.

**Visual**

Show `Model + GPU changed together → Cause unresolved`, then `Decision + reasons + history → Explanation effect not isolated`.

Animate a final-test box moving into the development loop after feedback is used; add a new protected evaluation box.

Excerpts: “The coding model is confounded with GPU class” and “This control does not distinguish the effects of the panel decision, reasons, and retained history.”

**Sources:** [Segmentation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10491), §3.2, final paragraph; [oversight study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28614), §6, paired retry-only comparison; [tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I), source timestamp **11:02.58–11:14.34**, `s00144–s00146`, and **11:22.74–11:41.74**, `s00149–s00153`. Small-set uncertainty also appears in the reviewed brief’s limitations.

### Scene 7 · 4:05–4:40 · What should change confidence?

<!-- claim_ids: 03-c1, 03-c2, 03-c3, 03-c4, 03-c5, 03-c6 -->

**Narration**

For your next experiment, delegate a narrow loop with a fixed budget. Keep evaluation authority separate, predeclare repetitions, preserve failures, and check the winner on evidence the search did not control.

This is an editorially inferred protocol, not a defense package experimentally shown to eliminate false conclusions.

The developments worth watching are reproducible transfer, complete cost accounting, and stronger verification. Those are the kinds of evidence that should change confidence in an agent’s result.

**Visual**

Return to the workflow diagram with protected evaluation and an archive attached. End card: **Watch for: reproducible transfer · complete costs · stronger verification**. Persistent label: **Editorial interpretation; uncertainty remains**. Cite Scenes 1–6 and their source locators; no invented result dashboard.

### YouTube description draft

What should students delegate to research agents—and what evidence should make their results trustworthy?

Research Loop presents a practical, editorially inferred protocol: choose a measurable bottleneck, protect evaluation, budget the complete comparison, fix repetitions in advance, preserve failures, and test transfer. This protocol has not been experimentally shown to eliminate false conclusions.

As of: **2026-10-14 (UTC)**.

Companion article: **[UNPUBLISHED_ARTICLE_URL — insert only after publication]**

The evidence includes research preprints, an author report, a practitioner tutorial and commercially interested founder testimony. These have distinct evidentiary roles; they do not collectively establish independent replication. The tutorial’s lucky-rerun instruction conflicts with its fixed-attempt rule and is not recommended. No independent physical-lab performance validation is supplied.

Sources:

- [Reward Hacking Challenges Oversight of Autonomous Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28614), §§6 and 8.
- [Agora: Git as Shared Memory for Collective AutoResearch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094), §4.8 and Appendix A.
- [Insights from Autoresearch for Solar Panel Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10491), §§2–3.2.
- [NanoProteinLM author report](https://jojoml.github.io/blog/2026/nanoproteinlm-agenticls/), “What survived the human gate.”
